payload.objective: Audit inherited taxonomies of thought: is a taxonomy a structure already present in the texts (discovered) or a label imposed later (invented)? Use two leak-free designs: a sealed text (Mawangdui manuscript, buried 168 BCE) and a sealed reader (a language model trained only on pre-1931 text).

H-C1.claim: The six-schools taxonomy predicts where an unseen book falls better than era, region or genre taxonomies.
H-C1.decision: rank by chance-corrected score with 95% bootstrap interval; require agreement across instruments (lex, lex_tr) for a main claim

H-C2.claim: The instrument ranks chapters that scholars regard as Daoist-leaning (Guanzi: Neiye, Xinshu I-II, Baixin; Han Feizi: Jie Lao, Yu Lao) high on Daoist affinity within their own books.
H-C2.decision: PASS if mean target percentile >= 80 and permutation p < 0.05; otherwise the instrument fails validation and no main conclusion may be published

H-C3.claim: The sealed manuscript sits between Dao and Fa instead of falling cleanly into one school.
H-C3.decision: 'constructed' prediction holds if dominant label share < 0.70 OR mean margin below the 10th percentile of transmitted books; otherwise the 'real structure' prediction holds

H-W1.claim: A reader sealed in 1930 already separates what was later called analytic vs continental philosophy.

H-W2.claim: A modern reader separates the later label more sharply than the 1930 reader, beyond its general advantage on labels that already existed in 1930 (hindsight gap G > 0).

decision_rules_after_first_tournament: If the six-schools taxonomy leads AND the tomb test supports 'real structure': next experiment = extend the sealed-text test to the Guodian slips.

If the six-schools taxonomy leads BUT the tomb test supports 'constructed': rewrite the conclusion as 'school structure holds in Han-edited transmitted books but not out of sample'; prioritise the translation-arm rerun.
If an era, region or genre taxonomy leads: reopen the premise that the school is the basic unit; next experiment = school test within era strata.
payload.disclosure: Lab tooling (corpus builders, instruments, statistics, tools, policies) was written before this run. A pipeline smoke test with a throwaway labelling was run during tool development; it is not a reported result. All taxonomies, experiment choices, runs, critiques and conclusions below are produced by the Omnigent agents.

steps: 1. Historian verifies the 8-item background checklist with sources and records evidence.
2. Advocate A formalizes and freezes the Sima Tan six-schools taxonomy (class names must include exactly 'Daoist' and 'Legalist' for the defectors instrument; sealed units never labelled).
3. Advocate B freezes era and region rival taxonomies; Advocate A freezes the genre rival taxonomy (one taxonomy per dispatch).
4. Statistician runs defectors (H-C2 validation) on instrument lex, then lex_tr; PAUSE and report if validation fails.
5. Statistician runs tournament (H-C1) for six-schools/era/region/genre on lex; cross-checks six-schools + strongest rival on lex_tr (main claim requires instrument agreement per pre-reg).
6. Statistician runs tomb_test (H-C3) on lex with the six-schools taxonomy.
7. Skeptic critique plus free controls: corpus_map, recognition probe via prober_a/prober_b + probe_score.
8. Auditor citation/overclaim check; planner writes the decision entry applying the pre-registered decision rules; then STOP and wait for the human scientist.
constraints: The two sealed excavated units (Huangdi_Sijing, Sun_Bin_Bingfa) must never be labelled by any taxonomy or used to fit any taxonomy.
Pre-registered hypotheses, thresholds and decision rules (r0002) are not modified.
Any paid control beyond the 9-credit PHASE 1 cap requires human approval; PHASE 2 keeps >= 7 credits.

payload.title: Composition-date era taxonomy (rival to inherited six schools)
payload.source_claim: Proposed by the Six Schools Lab advocate, 2026-10-03, in this dispatch conversation, as a rival hypothesis to the inherited six-schools taxonomy. Era boundaries follow standard periodizations of early Chinese intellectual history; per-book datings follow standard reference scholarship of the type surveyed in Michael Loewe (ed.), Early Chinese Texts: A Bibliographical Guide (1993), with later specialist studies including Brooks & Brooks, The Original Analects (1998), Yuri Pines, 'Dating a Pre-Imperial Text: The Case Study of the Book of Lord Shang' (2016), and the cited reference articles. CODEBOOK RULE (pre-registered): layered/compilatory texts (Analects, Liji, Guanzi, Kongzi Jiayu, Zhongyong, Liezi, Guiguzi) are assigned by the date of final compilation/redaction of the RECEIVED text as reported by the cited reference, not by their earliest stratum; where cited scholarship genuinely diverges, the assignment is marked contested. Sealed excavated units (Huangdi_Sijing, Sun_Bin_Bingfa) are never labeled.

payload.claim: Froze taxonomy 'era' (sha256 da4f2616ace3e71d95e427ef7d7d415a8f0d29aceebafac15f7233881596c1ab) as a composition-date rival to the six-schools taxonomy. Rationale: four era classes (Early and mid Warring States c. 480-350 BCE; Late Warring States c. 350-221 BCE; Qin-Han 221 BCE-220 CE; Post-Han c. 220-420 CE) with every transmitted book assigned from published datings, not stylistic reading. Pre-registered codebook rule for layered/compilatory texts: assign by final compilation/redaction of the received text per the cited standard reference, not earliest stratum.
disputed: Analects (final form mid-Han vs Brooks & Brooks ~315 BCE)
Xiaojing (late Warring States vs early Han)
Laozi (Guodian bundles vs consolidated mid-3rd-c. BCE text)
Liutao (Warring States final composition vs Han material)
Guanzi (Liu Xiang 26 BCE compilation vs late-Warring-States bulk per Sato)
Kongzi Jiayu (Wang Su 3rd-c. CE received text vs Han tomb evidence)
Zhongyong (Qin-Han editing vs Warring States dating)
Sunzi Bingfa, Wuzi (composition horizons genuinely unresolved)

payload.claim: Sima Tan's essay on the six schools is preserved in Shiji ch. 130 ('Yaozhi' / Essential Meanings / Lun liujia yaozhi 論六家要旨); Sima Tan died 110 BCE and the Shiji was completed by Sima Qian c. 91 BCE, so the essay dates before 110 BCE and was incorporated ca. 100-91 BCE. Its six categories are 陰陽家 Yinyangjia (Yin-Yang/Naturalist school), 儒家 Rujia (Confucians/Literati), 墨家 Mojia (Mohists), 名家 Mingjia (School of Names / 'names' specialists), 法家 Fajia (Legalists / fa school), 道家 Daojia (Dao school/Daoism). The essay is an argument favoring Daojia and coins several jia labels as novel evaluative categories rather than historical self-descriptions; whether 'Mingjia' maps onto the later 'School of Names' (bianzhe/disputers) is a retrospective and debated equivalence (Smith 2003; Fraser SEP 'School of Names').
payload.caveat: The 'ca. 100 BCE' date is approximate: the essay itself predates Sima Tan's death in 110 BCE, while the Shiji compilation incorporating it is c. 91 BCE; precise composition date is unverifiable.

payload.claim: The Hanshu Yiwenzhi (Ban Gu; Hanshu finished 111 CE, incorporating the bibliographic project Liu Xiang began in 26 BCE and his son Liu Xin completed in the Qilüe by c. 5 CE) classifies learning into six major divisions, with the Masters (Zhuzi) division listing ten schools: Sima Tan's six plus 縱橫家 Zonghengjia (Diplomatists), 雜家 Zajia (Syncretists), 農家 Nongjia (Agriculturists), and 小說家 Xiaoshuojia (Minor Talks), of which only nine are counted as worthy 'streams' (jiuliu 九流), Xiaoshuojia being excluded. Unlike Sima Tan's doctrinal evaluations, the Yiwenzhi is a bibliography that assigns texts to lineages and derives the schools from purported Zhou government offices.
payload.caveat: Precise institutional dating of the Qilüe layers (Liu Xiang's Bielu vs Liu Xin's redactions) is scholarly inferred; Ban Gu's 111 CE completion date is secure but the Yiwenzhi's dependence on Liu Xin is reconstruction from fragments.

payload.claim: Many transmitted masters texts were collated into (something like) their present form by the Western Han imperial library project: Liu Xiang, from 26 BCE at Emperor Cheng's command, organized, edited and abstracted the imperial library (Bielu), assisted by Liu Xin who completed the work. The received Guanzi is explicitly Liu Xiang's c. 26 BCE compilation of 86 pian; the received Zhanguoce and other texts are also his editions; Pines (2016) shows the received Book of Lord Shang likewise reflects Han-era transmission/collation.
payload.caveat: Extent varies by text: some received works (e.g., Han Feizi at 55 pian) appear substantially stable since Han cataloguing, while Guanzi is a heavy Han editorial product; 'Liu Xiang made the present text' must not be generalized to all 23 corpus books without text-by-text evidence.

payload.claim: Smith 2003 ('Sima Tan and the Invention of Daoism, "Legalism," et cetera', Journal of Asian Studies 62.1: 129-156) argues that Sima Tan's six jia labels, especially 'Daojia' and 'Fajia', are ad hoc early-Han rhetorical inventions, not descriptions of pre-existing self-aware schools, and that later bibliography (Liu Xin/Ban Gu) reified them. Csikszentmihalyi & Nylan 2003 argue that early Chinese intellectual lineages and teacher-student transmission chains are largely retrospective Han-era constructions built around exemplary figures. IMPORTANT BIBLIOGRAPHIC CORRECTION: the second article was published in T'oung Pao 89.1-3 (2003): 59-99 as 'Constructing Lineages and Inventing Traditions through Exemplary Figures in Early China', NOT in Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies and not under the title/subtitle given in the checklist.
payload.caveat: The constructivist theses are confirmed as real, influential scholarship, but the checklist's citation details for the Csikszentmihalyi & Nylan piece (journal and title) are wrong and must be corrected before the pre-registered documents rely on them.

payload.claim: Mawangdui tomb 3 was sealed in 168 BCE; its occupant was a male in his thirties, a son of Chancellor Li Cang (Marquis Dai) and Lady Dai (Xin Zhui), plausibly Li Xi; the silk manuscripts including the four texts behind the so-called Huangdi Sijing were excavated there in December 1973. Tang Lan (1974) first identified the four texts (Jingfa, Shidajing/Shiliujing, Cheng, Daoyuan) as the lost Huangdi Sijing listed in the Yiwenzhi under Daojia; most scholars accept this, but a significant minority prefer neutral labels 'Huang-Lao boshu' or 'Huangdi shu'. Composition datings proposed range from mid/late Warring States (late 4th c. BCE, per Tang Lan and others citing Shen Buhai/Huang-Lao references) to Qin/early Western Han (early 2nd c. BCE); the burial gives only a firm terminus ante quem of 168 BCE.
payload.caveat: Both the identification ('Huangdi Sijing' vs generic Huang-Lao silk texts) and the composition date (Warring States vs early Han) remain genuinely disputed, so the sealed-text corpus must use neutral descriptive names and treat only the 168 BCE burial as certain.

payload.claim: The Guanzi was classified under the Daoist (Daojia 道家) category in the Hanshu Yiwenzhi, but from the Sui shu bibliography onwards it has been placed in the Legalist (Fajia 法家) section, a reclassification maintained in later imperial catalogues (e.g., Siku Quanshu's Legalist section).
payload.caveat: The direction of the move (Daoist -> Legalist) is confirmed, but the lab should verify the exact Sui/Tang catalogue wording against Rickett's Guanzi introduction or the catalogues themselves, since my confirmation comes via a secondary article text ('Psychology and Self-Cultivation in Early Taoistic Thought') rather than the catalogue entries directly.

payload.claim: (a) Guanzi chapters Neiye 內業, Xinshu shang/xia 心術上/下 and Baixin 白心 are supported by scholarship as a Daoist-leaning 'inner cultivation' cluster: Harold Roth's Original Tao (Columbia UP, 1999) treats Neiye as a mid-4th-c.-BCE foundational early Daoist mystical text and analyzes these 'Techniques of the Way' chapters together; the Guanzi's own Han classification under Daojia (Yiwenzhi) corroborates the association. (b) Han Feizi chapters Jie Lao 解老 (ch. 20) and Yu Lao 喻老 (ch. 21) are widely described as the earliest extant Laozi commentaries, hence Daoist-leaning, though commonly judged later addendums distinct in ideology, lexicon and style from the rest of the Han Feizi.
payload.caveat: 'Daoist-leaning' is itself a retrospective label: constructivists (Smith 2003; Csikszentmihalyi & Nylan 2003) deny these chapters witness a self-aware 'Daoist school', and the authorship/dating of both the Guanzi cultivation chapters and the two Han Feizi commentary chapters is debated, so they are validator hypotheses, not ground truth.

payload.title: Regional-origin taxonomy of early Chinese thought texts (six regions)
payload.source_claim: Proposed by the Six Schools Lab Advocate on 2026-10-03 as an experimental rival to Sima Tan's inherited six-schools taxonomy: instead of 'school', each transmitted book is labelled by the regional culture of its traditionally attributed author or principal place of compilation, following Shiji-rooted attributions and modern regional-culture scholarship (Qi/Jixia academy studies, Chu-southern Daodejia culture, Qin Legalism, Lu-Zou Confucian-Mohian milieu, Central Plains Jin-successor states, and Wu-Yue military tradition). Attribution rule: assign the region of the traditionally attributed author's origin or service; when the attributed author is legendary or disputed, assign the region of the dominant place-of-compilation account and mark 'contested'.

payload.claim: Froze rival regional-origin taxonomy 'region' (sha256 34cd920f42e23a2efd64557c3d52f9e46bd03e75c0fb67f89b0f95ed747e78cd): 23 transmitted zh books labelled by regional culture of traditionally attributed author / dominant place of compilation, as a rival to the inherited six-schools taxonomy. Attribution rule: attributed author's origin or service region; for legendary/disputed attributions use dominant place-of-compilation account and mark contested. Sealed units Huangdi_Sijing and Sun_Bin_Bingfa left unlabelled.

classes.Lu-Zou: Analects, Mencius, Liji, Xiaojing, Kongzi_Jiayu, Zhongyong, Mozi

payload.disputed: Zhuangzi (Song birth vs Chu tradition), Mozi (Lu vs Song), Sunzi (Qi origin vs Wu service), Huainanzi (Chu court vs Jixia inheritance), Guanzi (Qi minister attribution vs anonymous multi-author Jixia compilation), Guiguzi/Liutao/Wei_Liaozi (legendary or poorly evidenced attributions).

payload.claim: Prior computational/DH work on early Chinese texts exists and must be cited rather than claimed as novel: (1) Nichols, Slingerland, Nielbo, Bergeton, Logan & Kleinman 2018, 'Modeling the Contested Relationship between Analects, Mencius, and Xunzi: Preliminary Evidence from a Machine-Learning Approach', JAS 77.1: 19-57 (ML text analysis of Confucian corpus); (2) Slingerland et al. related multi-year Chinese text-mining projects and Sturgeon 2018 automated text-reuse detection across transmitted early Chinese texts; (3) Allen, Luo, Murdock & Pu 2017 topic modeling of the HanDian ancient classics corpus; (4) Duan, Wang, Yang & Su 2023 network/DH analysis of cultural evolution of ancient China; (5) Wu & Wang 2025 quantitative semantic-boundary analysis of four ancient Chinese philosophies; (6) Hua 2025 stylometric study of the Zuo Commentary authorship controversy.
payload.caveat: These studies cover ML authorship/attribution, topic modeling, text reuse, clustering and semantic analysis of transmitted corpora, but none appears to combine taxonomy-blind sealed excavated manuscripts (Mawangdui, Yinqueshan) with transmitted texts as a held-out validation set, which is where the lab's design could be genuinely novel.
